cases.doctrine: The Court reiterated the two pactum commissorium elements — a pledge/mortgage securing a principal obligation and a stipulation for automatic appropriation by the creditor upon nonpayment — and held that the Memorandum of Agreement and Dacion in Payment constituted pactum commissorium and were void on that basis.
cases.examUse: Substance prevails over the label “dacion en pago”: ask whether the debtor truly made a later voluntary transfer independent of the security, or whether the transfer was prearranged to vest collateral automatically upon default.
cases.facts: Borrowers executed loan/security documents and later documents characterized as a dacion en pago after default. The creditor argued the arrangements were not an unlawful automatic appropriation.
cases.issue: Did the documents constitute a prohibited pactum commissorium under Art. 2088?
cases.name: Ong v. Roban Lending Corporation
cases.ruling: The Memorandum of Agreement and Dacion in Payment were held to constitute pactum commissorium and were declared void.

cases.doctrine: Dragnet clauses are capable of securing future indebtedness but are subject to strict construction. The reliance-on-the-security test examines whether the later credit was granted in reliance on the original mortgage or was treated as supported by a separate security; a new security can be evidence against extending the old mortgage to that loan.
cases.examUse: Do not say every future debt is secured because a mortgage contains a broad clause. Compare the first mortgage, later promissory note, later collateral, wording and evidence of the lender's actual reliance.
cases.facts: A bank sought to apply an earlier real estate mortgage's blanket clause to later credit accommodations, while the later transaction had separate documentation/security.
cases.issue: Does the dragnet clause cover the subsequent loan?
cases.name: Prudential Bank v. Alviar
cases.ruling: The Court applied strict construction and the reliance-on-the-security test to determine whether the later credit was covered by the original mortgage.

cases.doctrine: The Court upheld the after-acquired clause in the specific context of property acquired as additions/replacements in the business and expressly made subject to the lien, discussing immobilization and the parties' express treatment of the assets as subject to the real estate mortgage. Do not generalize it into a rule that every after-acquired movable automatically becomes real property.
cases.examUse: State the exact clause; examine the nature/use of the asset, whether it replaces/adds to mortgaged property, the parties' intent, and whether third-party rights/registration issues arise.
cases.facts: A lumber company mortgaged land, improvements and property used in the business. The deeds expressly covered replacement and subsequently acquired assets used in connection with the concession.
cases.issue: Can after-acquired property be covered by the real estate mortgage?
cases.name: People's Bank and Trust Co. v. Dahican Lumber Co.
cases.ruling: The clause covering replacement and subsequently acquired business assets was upheld in its specific context.

cases.doctrine: The Court distinguished equity of redemption from a right of redemption after a foreclosure sale. The general rule is that a post-sale right of redemption is associated with extrajudicial foreclosure; judicial foreclosure usually has no such post-confirmation redemption right unless a special statute grants it. Statutory bank-mortgage rights cannot be circumvented merely through assignment of the mortgage debt.
cases.examUse: Identify the foreclosure type, whether sale is confirmed/registered, the mortgagee's status and any banking-law exception. Never use “equity” and “right” of redemption interchangeably.
cases.facts: The dispute involved a mortgaged property and a claim to redeem after foreclosure, including the effect of assignment of the mortgage debt to an entity that was not itself a bank.
cases.issue: When does the right of redemption exist, and is it the same as equity of redemption?
cases.name: Huerta Alba Resort, Inc. v. Court of Appeals
cases.ruling: Equity of redemption was distinguished from a post-sale right of redemption; assignment of the mortgage debt to a non-bank did not circumvent the statutory bank-mortgage redemption framework.

cases.doctrine: Surplus from foreclosure must be returned to the mortgagor after applying the proceeds to the secured obligation and legally chargeable amounts. A failure to return the surplus is not necessarily a loan or forbearance of money; interest is governed by the applicable rules on obligations/damages and relevant jurisprudence.
cases.examUse: Confirm the exact factual holding on surplus and interest from the class-assigned decision.
cases.name: Spouses Suico v. Philippine National Bank
cases.note: Reviewer paraphrase: the syllabus names this case for surplus with only a central-doctrine summary and no facts, citation, or holding detail (per R06 p. 4). Confirm the holding in the class-assigned decision.

flashcards.back: To secure fulfillment of a principal obligation — not to transfer ownership to the creditor. The security generally follows the obligation and is extinguished with it.
flashcards.front: Pledge/mortgage: what is the purpose of an accessory security contract?

flashcards.back: Generally indivisible: the whole collateral may remain liable for the unpaid portion until full satisfaction; part payment releases no proportional part absent law or agreement.
flashcards.front: Art. 2089: what does indivisibility of pledge/mortgage mean?

flashcards.back: (1) Property pledged/mortgaged for a principal obligation; (2) stipulation letting the creditor automatically appropriate the collateral on nonpayment. The stipulation is void; the security contract itself is not necessarily void entirely.
flashcards.front: Art. 2088: recite the two elements of pactum commissorium.

flashcards.back: Substance prevails over the label “dacion en pago”: the MOA and Dacion in Payment were held void as pactum commissorium. Ask whether a post-default transfer was truly voluntary and independent or prearranged automatic appropriation.
flashcards.front: Ong v. Roban: what defeats a “dacion en pago” label?

flashcards.back: Art. 1602 presumptive circumstances (e.g., grossly inadequate price, vendor in possession, extended redemption, retained price, seller pays taxes); Art. 1603 resolves doubt in favor of equitable mortgage. Label not conclusive — intent and circumstances control.
flashcards.front: When is a “sale with right to repurchase” treated as an equitable mortgage?

flashcards.back: Capable of securing future advances but strictly construed — intent must be gathered from the instrument. Reliance-on-the-security test (Prudential Bank v. Alviar): was the later loan granted in reliance on the old mortgage, or on separate new security?
flashcards.front: Dragnet clause: construction rule and the reliance test?

flashcards.back: Only in its specific context: assets acquired as additions/replacements in the business and expressly made subject to the lien. It is NOT a rule that every after-acquired movable becomes real property.
flashcards.front: Dahican: what is the limit of the after-acquired property holding?

flashcards.back: Judicial: court action under Rule 68; equity of redemption before confirmation; generally no post-confirmation redemption. Extrajudicial: special power of sale + Act 3135 procedure; typically a one-year statutory right of redemption from registration of the certificate of sale.
flashcards.front: Contrast judicial vs. extrajudicial foreclosure on authority and redemption.

flashcards.back: Equity of redemption: pay to stop judicial foreclosure before confirmation. Right of redemption: statutory post-sale right, generally tied to extrajudicial foreclosure (Huerta Alba). Never use the terms interchangeably; banking-law exceptions and assignment issues may apply.
flashcards.front: Equity of redemption vs. right of redemption?

flashcards.back: Surplus belongs to the mortgagor (or persons entitled) after the secured obligation and lawful charges; the mortgagee may not divert it to unrelated unsecured debts. Non-return is not necessarily a loan/forbearance; interest follows obligations/damages rules (Suico).
flashcards.front: Foreclosure surplus: who gets it, and what about interest?

flashcards.back: Delivery to the creditor or an agreed third person is constitutive (Art. 2093); ownership stays with the pledgor. Against third persons, the pledge needs the required public instrument/description and Art. 2096 conditions.
flashcards.front: Pledge: delivery rule and effect against third persons?

flashcards.back: Public auction under Arts. 2112–2119 (notice, sale, application of proceeds). The pledgee cannot take ownership automatically — the auction is part of the anti-pactum-commissorium safeguard.
flashcards.front: How is a pledge foreclosed, and why an auction?

flashcards.back: First identify the statutory relationship (e.g., Arts. 1944, 1951, 1994, 2004, 546, 1731 — deposit, lease, repair, work), then apply the Arts. 2121–2122 retention/foreclosure rule.
flashcards.front: Legal pledge: what is the exam method?

flashcards.back: Sec. 7 reasonable-description rule: the instrument must describe the property sufficiently to identify it, plus affidavit of good faith and registration for effect against third persons. A vague catch-all may fail to identify collateral or bind third parties.
flashcards.front: Chattel mortgage: what does Act No. 1508 require for third-person effect?

flashcards.back: Pledge: possession delivered to pledgee/third person. REM and chattel mortgage: possession usually remains with the mortgagor. Automatic appropriation on default is prohibited (Art. 2088) in all three.
flashcards.front: Pledge vs. REM vs. chattel mortgage: who holds the collateral?

flashcards.back: Chattel foreclosure follows Act 1508: equity of redemption under the law, but no right of redemption after a completed sale (subject to special rules). Art. 1484's no-deficiency bar applies when the seller elects foreclosure in covered Recto installment sales — not to every ordinary loan chattel mortgage.
flashcards.front: Chattel mortgage: redemption rule and the Recto deficiency bar?

provisions.explanation: Common requisites of pledge and mortgage: constituted to secure a principal obligation; pledgor/mortgagor must be absolute owner (subject to rules/exceptions) with free disposal or legal authority; secured obligation must be valid though future/conditional obligations may be secured as allowed; the contract does not vest ownership in the creditor; the security is accessory and generally follows/is extinguished with the obligation.

Pledge and mortgage are generally indivisible even if debt or property is divisible: the whole collateral may remain liable for the unpaid portion until full satisfaction, subject to statutory exceptions; part payment does not automatically release a proportional part absent law or agreement.

Pactum commissorium: two elements — (1) property pledged/mortgaged for a principal obligation and (2) a stipulation letting the creditor automatically appropriate the collateral on nonpayment. The automatic-appropriation stipulation is void; the security contract itself is not necessarily void in its entirety.

REM directly and immediately subjects the identified immovable and covered rights/accessions to the secured obligation; ownership stays with the mortgagor subject to the encumbrance. Art. 2124: what may be mortgaged; Art. 2125: formalities/registration (validity between parties vs. effect against third persons); Arts. 2126–2127: direct security effect and extent including improvements/accessions. Present/future obligations may be secured when intended and legally compliant, but only obligations within the mortgage's scope.

Judicial foreclosure proceeds by court action: complaint pleading mortgage and default, court determination of amount due, foreclosure judgment; the Rules govern sale, confirmation, application of proceeds, and deficiency/surplus. Equity of redemption lets the mortgagor prevent completion by paying within the allowed stage/period before confirmation of sale. Generally no post-confirmation right of redemption unless a statute (e.g., banking law) grants it.

Extrajudicial foreclosure requires a valid special power to sell plus compliance with Act No. 3135: notice, publication, place/conduct of sale, bid, and registration must be tested. The purchaser's title is subject to a statutory right of redemption where granted — typically one year from registration of the certificate of sale, subject to special rules.

Pledge requires delivery of the movable to the creditor or an agreed third person (Art. 2093); ineffective against third persons absent the required public instrument/description and Art. 2096 conditions; only movables capable of possession may be pledged; ownership stays with the pledgor. Art. 2094 limits pledging future things; Art. 2095 covers fruits/products/accessories; Art. 2097 bars pledgor alienation without pledgee consent.

The pledgee holds the collateral with a right of retention for the secured debt until obligation and charges are paid; retention is not ownership and appropriation on default is barred. The Code addresses expenses, fruits, third-party claims, return of collateral, the duty to preserve (no use contrary to law/contract), debtor/third-party-owner redemption-or-return rights, and third-party-pledgor recourse/subrogation.

On nonpayment when due, the pledgee proceeds by the Code's public auction procedure: notice, public sale, and application of proceeds. The pledgee cannot become owner automatically (Art. 2088); the statutory auction is part of the anti-pactum-commissorium safeguard.

Legal pledge: the law gives a creditor a right to retain movable property for claims related to that property or service. Syllabus examples under Arts. 1944, 1951, 1994, 2004, 546 and 1731. Method: first identify the statutory relationship (e.g., deposit, lease, repair or work), then apply the relevant retention/foreclosure rule.

provisions.citation: Chattel Mortgage Law, Act No. 1508 (form and description)
provisions.explanation: A chattel mortgage secures debt with personal property while possession generally remains with the mortgagor, under Act No. 1508 and Civil Code Arts. 2140–2141: prescribed mortgage instrument/description, affidavit of good faith, and registration for effect against third persons. Sec. 7 reasonable-description rule: the document must describe the property sufficiently to identify it; a vague catch-all may not identify specific collateral or bind third parties. The mortgagor generally must own the property or be authorized to encumber it.

provisions.citation: Chattel Mortgage Law, Act No. 1508 (foreclosure and redemption)
provisions.explanation: Chattel foreclosure follows Act No. 1508 notice/public sale procedures and application of proceeds. The syllabus distinguishes equity of redemption under the law from no right of redemption after a completed sale, subject to any special rule. In Recto Law installment sales, Art. 1484's bar on deficiency recovery after the seller elects foreclosure is critical and does not automatically extend to every ordinary loan chattel mortgage.

Reviewer pointer only: the syllabus-cited RPC Art. 319 should be checked for fraudulent/specific chattel-mortgage acts in the fact pattern. The reviewer gives no elements or text; verify the article itself before applying it.

hints.conclusion: Automatic-appropriation stipulation is void; creditor must use legal enforcement. If a new, voluntary conveyance occurred after default, assess its independence rather than judging by label alone.
